newsitem.title: BELARUS: Lukashenko says row with Russia won't slow unity.
newsitem.headline: Lukashenko says row with Russia won't slow unity.

text.p: Belarussian President Alexander Lukashenko said on Tuesday that integration with Russia would go ahead despite a row with Moscow over the arrest of a Russian television crew.

Influential political critics in Russia would not distract him or Russian President Boris Yeltsin from their plans for unity enshrined in a treaty signed in May, Interfax-West news agency quoted him as saying in an interview.
"Neither he nor I will abandon the politics of integration," Lukashenko said.
The two presidents exchanged harsh words after the crew from Russia's state television channel ORT were arrested on July 26.
Yeltsin threatened to review the union treaty if the three-man crew, charged with illegally crossing the border from Lithuania, were not released. Two of the three face a possible five-year sentence.
Sounding a conciliatory note on Tuesday, Lukashenko said he was ready to meet Yeltsin to discuss problems relating to integration, though he added that it was not he who had started the argument.
"I did not start this kitchen row, this confrontation. If there are problems, I am ready to discuss them," he said.
Lukashenko was quoted as saying he did not intend to force the subject by asking for an urgent meeting but if Yeltsin wanted talks he was ready to meet at any time.

In a sign of the tensions stoked by the detention of the crew, Lukashenko angrily cancelled a visit to a Russian region last Friday after its governor urged a delay because of concern over the arrests.
Yeltsin said he did not believe the spat would worsen relations but that the row showed Lukashenko, 42, was "young and over-sensitive to criticism".
International human rights groups, often critical of press curbs in Lukashenko's former Soviet republic of 10 million people, have also urged the release of the Russian crew.
The mother of correspondent Pavel Sheremet sent a letter to Yeltsin, U.S. President Bill Clinton and international organisations on Tuesday seeking their help.
An ORT spokesman in Minsk said Sheremet's mother had said she was worried that charges would be made up against her son, accused by Lukashenko of being in the pay of unnamed foreign powers.

Earlier this year Kremlin liberals persuaded Yeltsin to water down the union treaty with Belarus, fearing that Minsk's lack of market reforms could hold Russia back. They also want to avoid giving Lukashenko a political platform in Russia.
Lukashenko has accused Russia's liberal First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais of trying to torpedo integration.
A spokesman for Lukashenko's administration said on Tuesday that a European Union mediator had arrived in Minsk to renew three-way talks with the president and the opposition.
The opposition, grouped around deputies who set up an alternative parliament after the old one was disbanded by Lukashenko, want new parliamentary elections to be held.
